747a09fe869ee9de: MELAKA: The memories of her two children, who died in a road accident in January 2023, remain close to the heart of Pakatan Harapan candidate for Rim, Esma Eazreen Husin.
Her late son, Hijjaz Kasturi Ramli, 19, and daughter, Nurul Fatihah Ramli, 21, shared her passion for community and political activities, often accompanying her to programmes and events.

Esma, 45, said she often wondered how excited they would have been to join her on the campaign trail had they still been around, especially her eldest child, who was usually the first to volunteer to accompany her to programmes around the constituency.

"If they were still here, I believe they would definitely accompany me to programmes. My eldest, Nurul Fatihah, was always the first to volunteer to join me at any programme around the state constituency.
"They loved helping out, and I believe they would also be enthusiastic about joining me on the campaign trail," she said when met at the PH main operations room in Bukit Baru here today.
The Melaka PKR Wanita vice-chief said losing both children had changed her life, with memories of them continuing to surface in her daily routine.
She said she chose to keep herself occupied with community and party activities, as spending too much time at home often brought back memories of her children and intensified her grief.
"That is why I keep myself busy with community and party activities. To some extent, they help take my mind off the sadness.
"At the same time, I get the opportunity to hear directly about the problems and needs of the people," said Esma, who is also Jasin PKR division deputy chief.
Among the memories she holds dear are photographs of her children after they cast their first votes in the 2021 Melaka election.
She said both had voted for the first time in the election, and she continued to treasure the photographs as a reminder of that moment.
"I still keep the photographs of them after they voted.
"Whenever I look at those pictures, so many memories come flooding back. They are also among the things that give me strength to continue campaigning and meeting voters," she said.
Despite her personal loss, Esma is now focused on the campaign, with water supply problems in Kampung Seri Kesang and Felda Kemendor among the main issues she hopes to address if elected.
Making her electoral debut, she is contesting against incumbent Rim assemblyman Datuk Khaidhirah Abu Zahar of Barisan Nasional.
In the previous election, Khaidhirah retained the seat with 4,037 votes and a majority of 1,327, defeating Perikatan Nasional candidate Azalina Abdul Rahman and PH candidate Prasanth Kumar Brakasam.
7366267ce954eb56: KUALA LUMPUR: A 20-year-old man who has lived in this country since he was three months old has failed in his bid to obtain citizenship despite DNA evidence confirming that his biological father is Malaysian.
The Kota Baru High Court dismissed Muhammad Fikri Salhan's application after finding that there was no evidence that his Malaysian father and Thai mother's marriage had been registered in Malaysia.

Judicial commissioner Tengku Amir Zaki Tengku Abdul Rahman ruled that Fikri was considered an illegitimate child for citizenship purposes, making his mother's nationality the determining factor in his application.
The judge said no documentary evidence had been produced to establish a valid marriage between Fikri's parents at the time of his birth.

He said Section 17 of Part III of the Second Schedule to the Federal Constitution was therefore applicable, under which references to the father or parents of an illegitimate child must be construed as references to the mother.
According to the grounds of judgment, Fikri was born on June 5, 2006, at a house in Golok, Thailand.
His birth was never registered with the Thai authorities, leaving him without a birth certificate.
When he was three months old, his father brought him to Malaysia, where he has lived ever since.
His biological mother could no longer be contacted, while his father was unable to recall the date of their marriage or produce any marriage documents.

Fikri and his father filed an originating summons seeking a declaration that he was entitled to Malaysian citizenship by operation of law, naming the National Registration Department director-general, the home minister and the government as defendants.
The plaintiffs relied on a DNA report issued by the Chemistry Department on Jan 12 this year, which they said conclusively established their biological relationship.
They argued that the evidence was sufficient to establish Fikri's entitlement to citizenship through his father under the principle of jus sanguinis, or citizenship by descent.
They also argued that administrative requirements should not override scientific evidence establishing biological parentage.
However, the court said the legal status of the parents' marriage at the time of birth was crucial in determining citizenship by operation of law.
"The court is satisfied that Fikri was born when there was no valid marriage between his parents.
"The determination of Fikri's citizenship status must depend on his mother's nationality.
"The court finds that Fikri has failed to prove that he is entitled to citizenship by operation of law under Article 14(1)(b) of the Federal Constitution," the court said.
The court dismissed the application with RM4,000 in costs.
51bcad54fcf093b7: KUALA LUMPUR: Kerajaan dicadang mewajibkan rakyat mengibarkan Jalur Gemilang mulai tahun depan sebagai tanda cinta dan kesetiaan kepada negara.

“Kalau dia benar-benar percaya kepada Allah dan kewujudan tuhan, dia tidak akan berani mencuri atau menyakau duit rakyat,” katanya.

46588c3a719defdf: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 4 — Former Undang Luak of Sungai Ujong Datuk Mubarak Thahak and five others today failed in a bid to halt committal proceedings against them after the Court of Appeal dismissed their application for a stay pending the disposal of their appeal.

A three-member panel comprising Justices Datuk Alwi Abdul Wahab, Datuk Dr Shahnaz Sulaiman and Datuk Amarjeet Singh unanimously dismissed the application and ordered the six appellants to pay RM60,000 in costs to the respondents, namely Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan (DKU) and its secretary, Raja Norazli Raja Nordin.

The six applicants, comprising four Undangs and two chieftains, had appealed against the Seremban High Court’s decision granting the DKU and Raja Norazli leave to initiate committal proceedings against them for allegedly breaching an injunction order.

The six appellants, besides Mubarak, are Undang Luak of Jelebu Datuk Maarof Mat Rashad, Undang Luak of Johol Datuk Muhammed Abdullah, Undang Luak of Rembau Datuk Abdul Rahim Yasin, Tunku Besar Tampin Tunku Syed Razman Tunku Syed Idrus Al-Qadri, and Shahbandar of Sungai Ujong Datuk Seri Badarudin Abdul Khalid.

Justice Amarjeet said that the committal proceedings directly involved the court’s jurisdiction to prevent undue interference with the administration of justice and to preserve the authority of the court in the public interest.
“In view of their nature, committal applications ought to be dealt with expeditiously in the interest of justice,” said Justice Amarjeet when delivering the bench’s decision.
He further said that the issue raised by the six concerning their purported immunity should be determined after, and not before, the substantive hearing of the committal proceedings.
“The very issue ought to be fully ventilated and determined at the committal proceedings during the substantive stage,” said the judge.

Justice Amarjeet also pointed out that the court found that the appellants had not approached the matter with clean hands, as they were seeking equitable relief while simultaneously pursuing a separate judicial review application at the Kuala Lumpur High Court concerning the same issues.

He said, more importantly, the appellants had failed to disclose to the High Court the existence of the injunction order and the fact that leave to commence committal proceedings had already been granted against them.

The legal dispute originated on May 5 this year when Mubarak and five others filed an originating summons at the High Court to obtain a copy of the minutes of a special DKU meeting held on April 17. Among the contents of the meeting minutes was a decision to remove Mubarak as Undang Luak of Sungai Ujong.

On June 5 this year, the High Court granted an ad interim injunction to preserve the status quo, maintaining the existing composition of the DKU and Raja Norazli’s position as its secretary, pending the determination of issues relating to jurisdiction and justiciability, or until further order of the court.

However, Raja Norazli claimed that media reports on the same day showed that the plaintiffs, particularly Maarof, had been involved in the purported appointment of the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan under Article 11 of the Negeri Sembilan State Constitution 1959, despite the injunction order still being in force.

He alleged that the appointment was made in defiance of the court order, prompting the DKU and Raja Norazli to seek leave from the High Court to commence committal proceedings against the six individuals for contempt of court. — Bernama

e23914479bc121f7: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 4 — Potager has received its first Michelin star in the fifth edition of the Michelin Guide Kuala Lumpur and Penang, announced today, while Dewakan retains its two stars.

The guide also includes nasi kandar for the first time: Hameediyah, established in 1907 and recognised by the Malaysia Book of Records as the country’s oldest nasi kandar restaurant, and Deens Maju, both in Penang, join the Michelin Selected list.
The 2027 selection features 159 establishments: one two-star restaurant, nine one-star restaurants, 60 Bib Gourmands and 89 Michelin Selected.
Last year’s edition listed 151 establishments, including 58 Bib Gourmands and 84 Selected.
Kuala Lumpur now has 80 establishments (77 last year) and Penang 79 (74 last year).
For the first time in Malaysia, the selection was announced through a press release rather than at a ceremony.

Michelin International Director Gwendal Poullennec said in a statement that the selection reflects “the continued importance of local favourites” alongside restaurants that combine Malaysian ingredients, regional flavours and international techniques.
The selection includes everyday dishes such as nasi kandar, koay teow th’ng and bak kut teh, alongside contemporary interpretations of local flavours.
Helmed by Chef Masashi Horiuchi, Potager has been on the Selected list for the last two years and earned its first star in this year’s Michelin Guide selection. — Picture courtesy of Potager
At the top of the list, Potager, a French contemporary restaurant in Kuala Lumpur’s Bamboo Hills led by Chef Masashi Horiuchi, earns its first star.
The restaurant opened in September 2023 and joined the Michelin Selected list in the 2025 edition and stayed on it last year before earning a star this year.
That brings the one-star total to nine, up from eight, with seven in Kuala Lumpur and two in Penang.

Dewakan retains its two stars, with Chef Darren Teoh the first chef to be featured in Michelin’s new Mindful Voices platform, which highlights the restaurant’s use of local, native and endemic ingredients to reduce imports.

Speaking to Malay Mail after the announcement, Teoh said, “I think in light of a hard season, we are thankful to continue to have guests who travel and see the vibrant and dynamic restaurant scene this country has. We think having a guide like the Michelin is great as a starting point for anyone who has never known the country before to begin to fall in love with it.”
Potager’s recognition also extends to its dining room: Nazahar, who has supervised service since the restaurant opened, received the Service Award. Three other special awards were presented.
Aidan Low, born in 1992, won the Young Chef Award for combining classical French technique and Japanese precision with native produce and house-made ferments at his Michelin-starred restaurant, Akar.
Joyin Goh of Tangram (Selected) won the Sommelier Award for a list of nearly 100 wines featuring lesser-known boutique wineries.

Root House by Gēn (Selected), Chef Johnson Wong’s restaurant at George Town’s 1926 Heritage Hotel, won Opening of the Year; it opened in July 2026 and explores Malaysian-Chinese cuisine through Hokkien, Teochew, Hakka, Cantonese and Hainanese traditions.

The Bib Gourmand list grows to 60 restaurants (26 in Kuala Lumpur, 34 in Penang), up from 58, with four new entries. In Kuala Lumpur, 7 Chai Ipoh Hor Fun serves classic Ipoh kai si hor fun, and Minji Bak Kut Teh serves bak kut teh made from an 80-year-old family recipe.

In Penang, Lemon Koay Teow Soup in Butterworth serves a unique pork-based koay teow th’ng with lemon juice, and Serabai Istimewa, which was among the selections dropped from the list last year, returns with its kuih serabai.

Two restaurants no longer appear on the list: Heun Kee Claypot Chicken Rice (Pudu) in Kuala Lumpur, which has closed, and Ah Boy Koay Teow Th’ng in Penang. A new claypot chicken rice restaurant, Yan Kee, has opened at the same location, run by the grandson of Heun Kee’s original owner.
Nasi kandar makes its long-awaited entrance in the Michelin Selected category, which has 89 establishments (46 in Kuala Lumpur, 43 in Penang), up from 84, with 12 new entries.
The iconic Penang dish ‘nasi kandar’ is included for the first time, with Hameediyah and Deens Maju joining the Selected restaurants in Penang. — Picture courtesy of Michelin Guide
Two nasi kandar institutions make the list: time-honoured Hameediyah on Lebuh Campbell, known for its kambing kurma and murtabah, along with another local favourite, Deens Maju on Jalan Gurdwara.

Penang’s other new entries are Flower Mulan, a florist-café serving Nyonya dishes that was among the restaurants dropped last year; Khaosan, a contemporary Thai restaurant serving “modern Thai tapas”; Root House by Gēn, the Opening of the Year winner; and See Kong Ooi, which serves home-style Malaysian-Chinese dishes in a restored heritage shophouse.
In Kuala Lumpur, six restaurants join the list, and three of them arrive with Michelin-recognised pedigree from elsewhere.
As I Am by Chef Ton, a contemporary Thai restaurant with views of Merdeka 118 and a 12-course tasting menu, was opened by Chef Thitid “Ton” Tassanakajohn, the chef behind Bangkok’s Le Du and Nusara.
Both restaurants hold one Michelin star in the Michelin Guide Thailand 2026, and his first Malaysian restaurant, Sood by Chef Ton in Penang, joined the Selected list in last year’s edition.
Jhol, which cooks the flavours of India’s nine coastal states, is an outpost of Bangkok’s Jhol, founded by Chef Hari Nayak, which is also listed in the Michelin Guide Thailand.
An outpost of Chef Hari Nayak’s Jhol in Bangkok, Jhol in Kuala Lumpur debuts among the Selected restaurants. — Picture courtesy of Jhol

Tangram, a contemporary Asian restaurant with French techniques and a seasonal tasting menu, is a collaboration between local partner Hsiao Tung Wei of Unwined and Chef Johnny Tsai, the creator of Taipei’s one-Michelin-starred T+T.

The other three additions in Kuala Lumpur are Merdeka Grill, a European restaurant in the newly opened Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur in Merdeka 118, serving dishes such as blue swimmer crab ravioli and Wagyu grilled over cedar wood; White N Black Kampong, a casual eatery serving kampung-style dishes for sharing; and Yellow Fin Horse, a contemporary Mediterranean restaurant in Else Kuala Lumpur.

Seven restaurants no longer appear on the Selected list. In Kuala Lumpur, they are K, Ling Long, Qureshi and Wagyu Kappo Yoshida, which have all closed; Potager left the category after moving up to a star. In Penang, they are Il Bacaro, Kota Dine & Coffee and Richard Rivalee.
Full list: Michelin Guide Kuala Lumpur and Penang 2027

d3140bfa455d8dce: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
Originally published on Global Voices
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home. Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.

Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia. Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed. According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800). For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable. He signed up and flew out.

What followed had nothing to do with brooms. Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine. He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign. Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons. When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there. Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.

His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain. But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.
A war that is running out of men

Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away. Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets. This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.

Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries. Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.

One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030. Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward. It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022. One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.

Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers. The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.
Who is accepting this offer?

Within South Asia, this recruitment scheme goes beyond just Bangladesh. After Sri Lanka’s economic collapse in 2022 and Nepal’s recession, wages of at least USD 550 a month in Russia looked like a way out, according to analysis from the Observer Research Foundation (ORF). Nepal’s foreign minister admitted in early 2024 that more than 200 Nepali citizens had been recruited. Kathmandu later suspended work permits for Russia after numerous Nepali citizens died on the front lines in Ukraine. Sri Lanka, for its part, saw an estimated 600 to 700 former soldiers recruited.

Why, then, would anyone take the risk? Money comes first. One welder, according to a report on survivors’ accounts, was offered a USD 20,990 signing bonus, a salary of USD 2,664 per month, and a shot at citizenship. For families buried in debt, those numbers can drown out the danger.

But money isn’t the whole answer. Some Bangladeshis enlisted knowingly were misled about the role, the reporting noted, while others lost a visa-linked job and found a recruiter waiting with a better-sounding contract. Some never aimed for Russia at all: One prisoner said an Uzbek broker had promised him residence in Italy. Once inside, the choice largely disappears, as recruits were presented with contracts in Russian, with those who hesitated facing threats and violence, according to Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds. Another report described passports and phones seized on arrival.
The legal door and the missing agreement

Russia was never a typical destination for Bangladeshi workers. This labor force first entered the country via shipyards, where skilled hands were needed as the war strained the domestic labor supply. Initially, around 56 workers were sent there. Then the flow increased. According to the data of the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), 993 Bangladeshis went in 2024 and 4,663 in 2025. The Bureau of Manpower Employment and Training (BMET) records 8,247 departures between 2024 and June 2026. The state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) sent just 426 among them, and those workers are reported safe; the private market carried the rest.

However, even with this sizable flow of workers, no signed labor agreement seems to exist between the two countries. During Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman’s June 2026 visit to Moscow, both sides merely urged early conclusion of pending accords, including a human resource agreement and a readmission agreement. Russia has agreed to fast-track a proposal for 100,000 Bangladeshi workers within a year. A state minister even spoke of 300,000 to 400,000 workers over five years. Meanwhile, Dhaka’s embassy in Moscow has asked Russia to bar Bangladeshis from military service.
The lack of a formal agreement leaves Bangladeshi workers exposed and vulnerable to scams and exploitation.
Fraud also shows up outside the war. In January 2026, 35 workers returned from Russia after being terminated, saying they had each paid about BDT 700,000 (roughly USD 5,651).
Agents, agencies, and the price of a seat

The route from village to barracks runs through ordinary offices. Bangladesh’s Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 30 men who flew to Russia in May 2026 went through three manpower firms, Jabal-e-Noor International, RS International, and TS Group. Officers arrested two alleged ringleaders in mid-October and say a Russian man and a Kyrgyz woman were part of the network, though these allegations remain unconfirmed. The expatriates’ welfare minister told Parliament that the men left with BMET clearance through licensed agencies, which shows that paperwork alone proves nothing.

Once the men landed, the script repeated. Their passports and phones were taken. After 21 days of training, they went to the front. Investigators said they were used as bait to expose enemy positions to drones.
Counting the dead without a count

Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited as of February 2026 and at least 34 killed, based on Ukrainian information, and warned that the real toll is probably higher. But on October 14, 2026, the SRB said 20 of the same 30 were dead, with 17 killed by a drone strike on their first day at the front and six still fighting, local news reports said.
These figures can’t simply be added together, because the overlap is unknown and the sources differ: police, rights groups, and Kyiv. Those families, meanwhile, wait without bodies.

Rights groups have urged Dhaka to dismantle the networks and Ukraine to screen captured foreign fighters for signs of trafficking. Yet families still ask for rescue, and the same daily’s editors have pleaded with the government to start bringing the stranded men home.
No Justice for the victims

Back to Maksudur Rahman: He got out, and today he sits at home in Lakshmipur, holding up a Russian military dog tag as proof of where he has been. Others from the same corner of Bangladesh haven’t come home. Sajjad, 20, was killed after being taken to fight, and his father, Mohammed Siraj, now holds a photograph of where his son used to be. For Siraj, justice is not an abstraction. It is a name on a charge sheet, a body to bury, and an answer to the question of who sent his son to war.

In the village, families confronted the recruiting agents and demanded to know why their loved ones were being trained for war. Their questions belong in a courtroom, not only in a village courtyard. Until the agents who sold these jobs and the system that cleared their paperwork are made to answer, the families will keep carrying a debt that is more than money.
Rahman’s loan was real, the war was real, and the janitor’s job never existed. A man who left home to earn a living came back carrying a soldier’s dog tag. And no justice in sight.
Written by Zulker Naeen

6b9b7cc24e0ea8b5: PETALING JAYA: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has called for urban development to prioritise the welfare of the people, particularly the poor and vulnerable, instead of focusing solely on modern buildings and infrastructure.
"When we talk about physical and urban planning, we are talking about life and humanity," he said at the launch of the Fifth National Physical Plan and Third National Urbanisation Policy today.
Also present were housing and local government minister Nga Kor Ming and federal territories minister Hannah Yeoh.
Anwar said the development of cities must also be guided by moral values, compassion and a commitment to uplifting disadvantaged communities.
He recalled visiting a settlement where residents faced poor living conditions, saying their circumstances served as a reminder of the government's responsibility towards the people.
"What is equally important is the welfare of the people, and that includes not just the elite but also those at the bottom," he said.
He also said that urban planning must give greater attention to public housing, hawker stalls, green spaces and basic amenities.
Anwar said about 80% of people visited stalls, warungs and small restaurants, but not enough attention was given to these places.
He said the success of urban development plans should be measured by how effectively they are implemented and whether they bring real improvements to people's lives.

He added that Malaysia must continue embracing technological advancements, including artificial intelligence and digital technology, to remain competitive.
However, he stressed that technological progress must not come at the expense of moral values, humanity and the welfare of the people.

2604656285de6706: WASHINGTON: Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and House on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories that reached deep into Republican strongholds as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to president Donald Trump.

The size and breadth of the Democratic wave were still coming into focus, but the party prevailed in states long thought to be out of reach, including conservative bastions like South Carolina, Texas and Iowa.

The Democratic wave underscored voters' deep frustration with Trump's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war against Iran in February, which drove gas prices up sharply. In poll after poll, voters expressed anxiety about the cost of living and anger at the way Trump has handled the issue.
In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since the Great Depression nearly a century ago.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown claimed a seat that belonged to vice president JD Vance two years ago, while Texas Democratic state Representative James Talarico withstood a barrage of outside spending to defeat scandal-plagued Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Ohio and Texas voted for Trump by a double-digit margin in 2024.

In South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, pediatrician Annie Andrews triumphed over Republican Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

Trump elevated Paxton and Graham ahead of more established candidates despite clear liabilities. Paxton has been at the center of a litany of controversies, including his 2023 impeachment and securities fraud charges, while Graham's admitted inexperience drew negative headlines.

Trump campaigned heavily for Paxton, Graham and Ohio's Jon Husted as part of a late election blitz that included more than two dozen rallies, and the president told his supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot" in an effort to fire up his base.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter".
Democrats had flipped six Republican Senate seats in all, ensuring a majority even if they don't manage to hold their own seats in competitive Michigan and Minnesota.

Democrats were also on track to take control of the US House of Representatives after flipping at least eight Republican seats in states including Kentucky, New Jersey and North Carolina and showing strength even in solidly conservative districts.

The party's dominance extended to other races as well. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent, lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Democrats also captured governorships in conservative Iowa and Ohio.
A rebuke to Trump, winner says

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named president Donald J Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about 3 percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats.
Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least 9 percentage points.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.
In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.
66999959cb880c83: Thailand's foreign minister said he will visit Myanmar on Nov 12, days before a regional summit where Bangkok will be pressing to normalise ties with the war-torn country.

Sihasak Phuangketkeow's trip also comes during raised tensions along the countries' shared border, where Bangkok said clashes between Myanmar's military and ethnic rebels caused property damage and injured a Thai civilian in Thailand on Thursday.
His visit, announced late Tuesday, is scheduled shortly before a Nov 16-18 summit of Asean leaders in Manila.

Myanmar's leaders have not been invited to high-level Asean meetings since former general Min Aung Hlaing led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war.
Sihasak told reporters in Beijing his government wants to "hear Myanmar's latest position" ahead of the summit.
"De-escalation by all parties will help create a conducive atmosphere for essential dialogue and the peace process," he said.

"If there is progress on these fronts, it will be a positive factor for Asean to consider at the leaders' summit, as we decide how to move forward on the situation in Myanmar, including Myanmar's participation in Asean meetings," he added.
Sihasak, who last visited Myanmar in April, said he would meet his counterpart, Tin Maung Swe, on Nov 12, and a meeting with Min Aung Hlaing was "in the works".
In July, Bangkok hosted a meeting between Tin Maung Swe and foreign ministers of several Asean member states, the first such gathering since the 2021 coup.
The following month, Min Aung Hlaing met with Thai prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul in Bangkok, with the two nations' military chiefs holding talks two weeks after.
Min Aung Hlaing took over as civilian president in April following elections widely dismissed by monitors as a charade.
Since then he has been given a red-carpet welcome across the region, in India, China and several Asean nations.
Myanmar is expected to send a senior civil servant to the Manila summit.
Thailand has stepped up security on its western frontier following last week's cross-border fire.

On Wednesday, Myanmar's military blamed "terrorist insurgents" – how it refers to ethnic-minority armed groups and pro-democracy forces – for wounding a Thai national, according to a statement in state media.
a8bbe36a4fa3b3c3: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 4 — Renowned education figure Tan Sri Dr Asiah Abu Samah died at a private hospital in the capital today. She was 89.
Asiah, the first woman to serve as Malaysia’s director-general of education, died at 5 am.
According to a circulated notice, funeral prayers will be held after Zohor prayers at Masjid At-Taqwa in Taman Tun Dr Ismail, followed by burial at the Bukit Kiara Muslim Cemetery here.
Born on March 1, 1937, in Parit, Perak, Asiah made significant contributions to the development and advancement of Malaysia’s education system.
She studied at Universiti Malaya in Singapore, where she obtained a Bachelor of Arts degree in History and a Diploma in Education before beginning her teaching career at Penang Free School in 1961.
She later served as a language lecturer at an institute in Lembah Pantai before being appointed principal of Tunku Kurshiah College (TKC) in Seremban, a position she held from Dec 1966 to Sept 1970.

Meanwhile, Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek described Asiah’s passing as a major loss to the nation’s education sector, particularly given her contributions to the development of the national education system.
“I am deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Tan Sri Asiah Abu Samah, former director-general of education.

“As the first woman to hold this position, she paved the way for women to take on leadership roles in the country’s education sector. Her contributions will always be remembered by those of us who continue the responsibility of educating Malaysia’s children,” she said in a Facebook post.
Fadhlina also extended her condolences to Asiah’s family on behalf of the Education Ministry.
“May her family be granted strength and patience as they cope with the loss of their loved one. May Allah SWT forgive her sins, bless her soul and grant her a place among the faithful.
“Thank you, Tan Sri, for your dedication and invaluable service to the nation’s education sector,” she said. — Bernama
bd4978760cc3457d: PETALING JAYA: Urban planning and development should not sideline humanitarian values and the welfare of the people, in line with the Malaysia Madani concept.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the efficiency and performance of the Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) should serve as an example in improving urban planning to ensure it is not focused solely on the grandeur of physical structures.
"When we talk about physical and urban planning, we are talking about life, humanity, and matters related to our faith in religion, values and morality.

"Sometimes, we go to work and return home, forgetting that urban development is actually about human development, as well as fostering our faith and morality, so that humanitarian principles remain at the core," he said.
The prime minister was speaking at the opening of World Town Planning Day 2026 and the launch of the Fifth National Physical Plan (RFN5) and Third National Urbanisation Policy (DPN3) today.
Also present were Housing and Local Government Minister Nga Kor Ming and Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh.
93812eb497c7fe43: ACTOR and director Khir Rahman is set to return to his roots, taking to the stage at Istana Budaya next month in the children's musical 'Pengembaraan Sang Kancil'.
This marks the 53-year-old artiste's first theatre show in nearly 10 years, following his performance in 'Semerah Padi'.
Khir will play Raja Rimba (King of the Jungle) in the three-day production, which opens on Nov 13 at Panggung Sari.
Reflecting on the opportunity, Khir has expressed delight at his comeback in a children's musical.

"Those who have followed my journey from the beginning know that my origins lie in theatre. Stage productions, festivals, and competitions have been part of my life since I was young," Khir told Bernama recently.
"Returning to the stage through a children's play feels like a true homecoming. It is right up my alley, especially since I previously worked on productions like Uda dan Dara."
Khir said working alongside child actors has brought him immense joy, praising their dedication and early head start in the performing arts.
Among the young cast is child actor Ahmad Zaid Ahmad Zaha, who plays the lead role of Sang Kancil.

"Even though Sang Kancil is small, he is brave. That's a huge motivation for me because I'm quite small compared to others at school. I want to be like Sang Kancil — small, but confident enough to speak up," said the Year 6 pupil.
'Pengembaraan Sang Kancil' tells the story of the clever mousedeer as he uses his quick wits to help oppressed animals and protect his family from the dangerous Taring.
Istana Budaya production director Hanida Mohamed Yusof described the show as a "Nusantara magic" concept, infusing regional folklore, live music, dance, and humour.
The production features 46 child actors and 16 original songs performed live by Orchestra Tradisional Malaysia and string players from the National Symphony Orchestra.
"We strongly believe that introducing the arts at an early age helps shape a lasting appreciation and love for culture and the arts among our children," Hanida said.
Directed by Nawfal Zamri, 'Pengembaraan Sang Kancil' runs from Nov 13 to 15. Tickets are available via Istana Budaya's social media platforms or by calling 03-4026 5555.

e9c2879d1e7d203a: WASHINGTON: Democrat Adam Hamilton won a US Senate seat in Kansas on Tuesday, according to US media projections, unseating Republican incumbent Roger Marshall and becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the largely rural, conservative state since 1932.

The result is a blow to President Donald Trump, who carried Kansas by more than 10 points in each of his three presidential campaigns and travelled there last week, his first visit to the state since 2018, to rally support for Marshall.
Hamilton, the pastor of a Methodist megachurch who was registered as a Republican until recently, had considered running as an independent before entering the race as a Democrat.

He campaigned as a moderate, kept his distance from national party leaders and pledged not to back Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader. He also criticised how former president Joe Biden's administration handled immigration.
Hamilton largely aimed his attacks at Marshall and congressional Republicans rather than the president.
"I'm not running against President Trump," he said at their final debate.
Marshall, by contrast, told voters that supporting him meant supporting the president's agenda.
The two men also clashed over tariffs. Hamilton called for ending Trump's tariffs and requiring congressional approval for any new ones, while Marshall insisted they were working.

Many Kansas farmers, already squeezed by fuel costs driven up by the Iran war, have been hit by retaliatory tariffs on exports such as soybeans and wheat. Cattle ranchers were angered by a Trump plan to ease tariffs on beef imports.
In rural Neosho County, where 73% of voters backed Trump two years ago, Hamilton's yard signs appeared in the final weeks of the campaign.
"I think people are just desperate for a bit of normalcy," Travis Falstad, 53, a left-leaning voter in the county, told AFP before the vote.
25ef5b48ae825e0e: KUALA LUMPUR: Seorang Ahli Parlimen Bersatu menyifatkan gelaran ‘dajal’ terhadap tujuh wakil rakyat pembangkang yang menandatangani Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan (CSA) dengan kerajaan sebagai tuduhan berat.
Suhaimi Abdullah (PN-Langkawi) berkata, label sedemikian menimbulkan persoalan mengenai kesungguhan pihak tertentu dalam memperjuangkan perpaduan nasional.
Katanya, usaha mencapai persefahaman demi kepentingan rakyat sukar direalisasikan jika Ahli Parlimen yang mengambil pendekatan bekerjasama turut dilabel ‘dajal’.
“Macam mana nak wujudkan perpaduan nasional jika kami (Ahli Parlimen pembangkang) yang menandatangani perjanjian (CSA) dipanggil dajal? Ini amat menyedihkan.

“Semalam, apabila saya pulang, anak-anak bertanya mengenai dajal. Saya kata Wallahua'lam, saya sedang mengkaji apa maksud dajal,” katanya ketika membahaskan Belanjawan 2027 peringkat jawatankuasa bagi Kementerian Perpaduan di Dewan Rakyat.

Suhaimi antara tujuh Ahli Parlimen pembangkang yang menandatangani CSA dengan kerajaan pada 29 Okt lalu, selain Presiden Bersatu Muhyiddin Yassin bersama lima lagi wakil rakyat parti itu serta Ahli Parlimen Muar daripada Muda, Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.
Semalam, Presiden PAS Hadi Awang menyifatkan perjanjian itu sebagai penipuan dajal atau ‘pembohong paling besar’, yang dalam Islam dikaitkan dengan tanda besar hampirnya kiamat.

Hadi mendakwa, CSA mencerminkan pendekatan dajal pada akhir zaman apabila kuasa digunakan untuk memaksa pihak tertentu bagi memastikan kerajaan terus berkuasa, bukannya dianggap sebagai amanah kepada rakyat.
Beliau turut berkata, parti yang membentuk kerajaan wajib menunaikan amanah kepada rakyat tanpa perlu membuat aku janji terlebih dahulu.
Perjanjian itu memberikan mereka akses kepada peruntukan pembangunan kawasan Parlimen, yang dinikmati wakil rakyat kerajaan sepanjang empat tahun lalu.

Sebagai balasan kepada sokongan mereka, Putrajaya perlu melaksanakan dua reformasi utama, iaitu mengehadkan tempoh jawatan perdana menteri serta memisahkan peranan peguam negara dan pendakwa raya sebelum tamat penggal Parlimen.

b0887ae57e847e53: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 4 — Two new blocks at Penang Hospital are expected to help ease congestion at its Emergency and Trauma Department, with the women’s and children’s block scheduled for completion in 2027 and the specialist clinics and wards block in 2029.
State Youth, Sports and Health Committee chairman Daniel Gooi Zi Sen said the projects formed part of the hospital’s long-term plan to address overcrowding caused by a shortage of ward beds.

He said the Health Ministry was also implementing measures under its patient flow management guidelines, including diverting non-emergency patients from the department through stronger primary healthcare services and better screening at entry points.

“These measures include extending the operating hours of health clinics to allow high-risk patients to be admitted directly to hospital wards, as well as working with nearby private clinics under the MADANI Medical Scheme and PeKa B40 for low-risk cases.”
Gooi was replying to Gooi Hsiao Leung (PH-Bukit Tengah), who asked about measures to address congestion and long waiting times at the department during the State Assembly sitting today.

Gooi noted that the ministry had also strengthened the Bed Management Unit, introduced the Open Bed Policy and expanded the use of multidisciplinary wards to ensure patients could be placed in any available bed.
He said discharge and post-treatment processes had also been streamlined through a Discharge Lounge, with a target of freeing up beds before noon to accommodate new patients.

Statistically, Gooi said the proportion of critical patients in the Red Zone rose to 7.14 per cent by July 2026, up from 6.79 per cent in 2025, while semi-critical Yellow Zone cases rose to 19.81 per cent from 18.92 per cent.

Green Zone cases remained almost unchanged at 40.06 per cent, compared with 40.13 per cent in 2025, while non-emergency cases (LOCUM) declined to 32.99 per cent from 34.16 per cent, he added. — Bernama

f1ea0988165f23c7: WASHINGTON, Nov 4 — Democrat James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminarian who campaigned on a “politics of love,” won the US Senate race in Texas, flipping yet another seat for his party in a huge blow to Republicans.
Talarico defeated the state’s attorney general Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who survived impeachment and years of scandal, NBC News and CBS News projected.
He becomes the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.
The result was a major setback for Trump, who threw his weight behind Paxton and made the state a campaign priority.
In another political earthquake for the southern border state, Democrat Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott.

Hinojosa, a 52-year-old attorney and state lawmaker, is part of a new generation of Democrats who are seeking to attract independents and voters disillusioned by Trump’s unpopular war in the Middle East and skyrocketing prices for gas and everyday goods.

The landmark victories for Democrats could signal that Texas, the country’s second most populous state with 40 electoral votes, is becoming competitive in national elections, a shift that could reshape the electoral map for future races.
The result also marks a defeat for tech billionaire Elon Musk, who became one of Talarico’s most vocal opponents in the final weeks of the campaign.
Musk, who has moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas, has a growing business stake in the state.
The world’s richest man spent more than US$200 million supporting Paxton, according to federal filings.

Talarico ran on a blend of Christian faith and economic populism, describing the contest in the final days of the campaign as a David versus Goliath fight and inviting Republicans dissatisfied with the party to join him.
“We are uniting Texans from all backgrounds and beliefs onto one team to take on this broken, corrupt political system,” he told reporters after voting early in Austin last week.
Trump traveled to Texas four times in the month before the election to rally for Paxton, whom he endorsed over four-term incumbent senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary.
At rallies, Trump told voters that a Democratic victory would mean open borders and economic damage, and repeatedly mocked Talarico.
The race became the most expensive non-presidential contest in US history, with more than US$560 million spent or reserved on political advertising, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
Top versus bottom

Talarico, a 37-year-old former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian, was elected to the Texas House of Representatives in 2018 and built a national following with speeches combining progressive politics, biblical teaching and criticism of wealthy elites.
A two-hour appearance on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2025 brought him an audience beyond traditional Democratic voters.
He defeated congresswoman Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary and sought to broaden his appeal by criticizing aspects of former president Joe Biden’s immigration policies.
His positions on abortion and LGBTQ rights drew sharp criticism from religious conservatives.
Paxton, 63, survived impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on allegations of corruption and abuse of power before being acquitted by the state Senate.
He has denied wrongdoing and portrayed his legal troubles as attacks by the political establishment.
During the campaign, Talarico drew support from voters who had left the Republican Party.

“That party’s crazy. They left me, I didn’t leave them. The MAGA people are crazy,” Noel, a 75-year-old lifelong Republican, told AFP at a recent rally in Galveston, a Republican stronghold on the Texas coast.
“He’s a young man, he’s an honest man, he’s got a vision, he’s smart, well-spoken, nice, kind, which is what we need,” he said.
Younger voters were also drawn to his campaign. Maya Guerra, the 21-year-old daughter of Latino migrants, told AFP in Houston that she saw Talarico as a source of hope.
Traci Gibson, head of the Democratic Party in Harris County, which includes most of Houston, said Talarico’s message reached across party lines.
“It’s not left, it’s not right. It’s top versus bottom,” she told AFP. “It is us versus corrupt billionaires. It is us with our health care. It is us with our gas prices.” — AFP

60ccf588d0128719: SINGAPORE, Nov 4 — The names of some Singapore Airlines (SIA) customers and their travel booking details were accessed without authorisation after airline technology provider Amadeus suffered a data breach.
Amadeus, which supports certain SIA reservations and booking processes, shared with Singapore’s flag carrier that data from about 46,000 SIA booking records was compromised.

An SIA spokesperson told AsiaOne that for about 620 booking records, additional information including email addresses, phone numbers, travel document details, and KrisFlyer membership numbers may have been accessed too.
The Spanish firm has confirmed to SIA that the exposed data does not include bank account or credit card information, and the unauthorised access also did not result in any modification to bookings.

“The incident was confined to Amadeus’ platform, and Amadeus has informed SIA that it has implemented containment measures and additional security safeguards following the incident,” the spokesperson added.
“SIA would like to assure all customers that the incident did not involve a breach of its IT systems.”

As a precaution, the carrier said it is directly contacting affected customers with upcoming travel to change their booking reference numbers, adding that it has informed the relevant authorities about the matter.
“SIA sincerely apologises to affected customers for any inconvenience caused,” the spokesperson said.
“The protection of our customers’ personal data is of utmost importance to SIA.”
Other global carriers affected by this data breach include Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, Korean Air and Malaysia Airlines.
According to a statement posted on Amadeus’ website in October, certain booking-display data was available through a software glitch.
It said its investigations are ongoing, and there is no evidence that payment or financial data was accessed.

Amadeus added that there are no signs the vulnerability has been exploited for ransomware purposes, and that it has since implemented measures to fix the vulnerability as well as enhanced monitoring and detection capabilities. — AsiaOne

883e252867e08983: COLUMBUS, Nov 4 — Democrat Amy Acton was elected governor of Ohio yesterday, defeating Republican Vivek Ramaswamy after a bitter contest in which he spent millions of dollars on deeply personal attack ads featuring her estranged mother, The Guardian reported.
Acton, 60, will become the first woman to serve as Ohio’s governor, ending 16 years of Republican control. She is also the first Democrat to win the post since Ted Strickland in 2006.
She succeeds the term-limited Republican Mike DeWine.
According to the report, the race became one of the most expensive and acrimonious in the United States in the final weeks before election day.

Ramaswamy’s campaign aired an advertisement featuring Acton’s mother calling her a liar. The Guardian reported that Acton’s mother had lost custody of her after Acton’s stepfather was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.
The advertisement drew criticism from politicians of both parties, who urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it and apologise.
However, US President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance backed the minute-long spot, on which the campaign said it would spend US$4 million. The advertisement was eventually pulled last week.
Acton, who led Ohio’s health department during the first months of the Covid-19 pandemic, campaigned on lowering living costs.

According to the report, her pledges included an earned income tax credit, a child tax credit of up to US$1,000, a public prescription drug platform and property tax relief for seniors and middle-income homeowners.
The report said she cast herself as a pragmatist who had served in a Republican administration under DeWine.

Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur, secured Trump’s endorsement on the day he launched his campaign. He promised to make Ohio income-tax free within a decade, cut energy bills and restore “law and order” to the state’s cities.
The Guardian described Acton’s road to victory as turbulent for a first-time candidate who, like Ramaswamy, had never held elected office.

Early polls showed her trailing by double digits, with roughly a quarter of voters saying they had never heard of her. For months, Democrats speculated that better-known figures, including former senator Sherrod Brown and former congressman Tim Ryan, might enter the race.

By mid-October, Ramaswamy and his allies had spent more than US$100 million on advertisements against Acton — roughly three times what her campaign spent — targeting her role in the state’s pandemic shutdowns, the report said.
At an October rally in Youngstown, Trump called Acton “a radical left lunatic”.
Polling nonetheless shifted steadily in her favour through the autumn, with a string of October polls showing her in the lead.

The Guardian noted that Acton will govern a state that backed Trump by 11 points in 2024, alongside a Republican-controlled legislature, setting up potential clashes over tax reform, school funding and data centres.

ca28bbe6e3dcc563: KUALA LUMPUR: Kerajaan sedang meneliti kemungkinan memberi perlindungan undang-undang khas kepada pensyarah di universiti awam melalui akta baharu bagi menjamin kebebasan akademik mereka.

20e43b3be28d45e1: LOS ANGELES: An aging Nasa satellite telescope that a robotic spacecraft was sent to retrieve on a failed rescue mission this summer was headed for a fiery re-entry into Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, nearly 22 years after it was launched into orbit.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, weighing roughly 3,200 pounds (1,452 kg), was set to tumble out of orbit and burn up in the atmosphere somewhere over the tropics, with fragments surviving re-entry unlikely to threaten populated areas, according to NASA.

The US Space Force has put the odds of harm coming to anyone on Earth at one chance in 2,100, NASA said in an online statement, projecting the time of re-entry at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST (0830 GMT). The Aerospace Corporation, a nonprofit national security research entity, projected a re-entry window of 5:19 a.m. EST, plus or minus two hours.

London-based astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, an honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre, cited revised US Space Force data predicting re-entry most likely to come around 7:45 a.m. EST.

"The satellite is in a very circular orbit, skimming the top of the atmosphere," he told Reuters by phone on Tuesday night. "The question is at what point does it heat up enough that it starts breaking up."

Nasa's prized US$500 million Swift satellite, a first-of-its-kind multi-wavelength space observatory, has been studying gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic phenomena since 2004, using its array of three telescopes.

The observatory, which has no onboard propulsion system of its own, has been drifting toward an expected demise for months as it circles the globe at a speed of roughly 17,000 miles per hour (27,359 kph).
Astronomers had hoped to extend Swift's mission for a number of years by giving the satellite telescope a lift.

In July, Nasa and Arizona-based startup Katalyst launched a specially built rescue vehicle called LINK on a mission to rendezvous with Swift, latch onto the satellite and tug the observatory back into a higher, more sustainable orbit.
But the LINK spacecraft itself began spinning uncontrollably soon after reaching space, and by mid-August, mission managers abandoned the effort, resigned to letting Swift continue to meet its fate.

The aborted rescue attempt, the first US mission of its kind, took on heightened significance as a demonstration of a new orbital grappling technology seen as pivotal to the outcome of the US-China space race.
The LINK effort was closely watched as a trial run of a key satellite-maintenance technology with potential dual-use military space applications.
Katalyst touted the mission as a historic endeavor that designed, built and tested the LINK rescue vehicle on an unprecedented nine-month production schedule under a Us$30 million Nasa contract.
Swift was launched more than two decades ago to explore the most powerful known explosions in the universe, bursts of gamma-ray radiation emanating from the cores of distant galaxies.

Originally designed for a two-year prime mission, Swift remained in operation far longer with observations of a wide range of cosmic objects, from galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars emitting X-ray flares, to comets and asteroids streaking through our own solar system.

c8ee1f5df1fab652: SINGAPORE, Nov 4 — A man who was seen taping his mobile phone to the rear of an SBS Transit double-decker bus has defended his actions amid online safety concerns, claiming he staged a stunt and that his phone was not attached to the bus.

2b4eb04d34055930: PETALING JAYA: Former Umno supreme council member Puad Zarkashi today questioned whether the party could be considered a "lesser Dajjal", the term used by PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang to describe the confidence and supply agreement (CSA) signed between the government and seven opposition MPs.
In a Facebook post, Puad said the party was part of the unity government that signed the CSA.
"According to Hadi, the 'lesser Dajjal' served the 'great Dajjal'. Does this mean Umno is the 'lesser Dajjal' as it is part of the unity government?"
The Dajjal is the great deceiver whose emergence is regarded in Islam as one of the major signs of the approaching Day of Judgment. He is also sometimes referred to as the anti-Christ.
Yesterday, Hadi likened the CSA between the government and seven opposition MPs to the Dajjal's deception.
He said Prophet Muhammad had warned that before the emergence of the great Dajjal, several "lesser Dajjals" would appear throughout the world.

"A CSA is Dajjal-like as power is no longer regarded as a trust that must be upheld for the benefit of all, but instead becomes a means of coercing others to ensure the government remains in power," the Marang MP was quoted as saying.

Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman and six MPs from Bersatu, led by former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, signed the CSA last Thursday, gaining access to constituency development funds that government MPs have had access to for the past four years.

The CSA also underlined two key reforms for Putrajaya to undertake in exchange for their support: limiting the prime minister's tenure and separating the roles of the attorney-general and public prosecutor before the end of the parliamentary term.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the CSA was open to all opposition MPs, while his deputy, Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, said the deal should be extended to other opposition parties.
Puad urged Umno's ulama council to state its stance on the matter.
He also questioned the apparent silence by several religious leaders in the party, like Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki and Khairuddin Aman Razali.

00a5529815b8622f: KUALA LUMPUR — Malaysia has secured its lowest-ever pricing spread on a dollar-denominated sovereign bond, after drawing more than US$9.5 billion (RM38.6 billion) in total demand for its global sukuk issuance, Parliament was told.

1d10ba553d7defb1: SAO PAULO, Nov 4 — A Sao Paulo state court ordered US tech giant Meta on Tuesday to stop collecting content to train its AI models from Brazilian media outlets in three national press associations.

The preliminary injunction, seen by AFP, comes after the associations filed a civil suit alleging that Meta – owner of Facebook, Instagram, Threads and Whatsapp – had demanded free access to content in exchange for continued use of its platforms.
The judge set a daily fine of one million reais (about US$180,000, or RM733,000) if Meta fails to comply.
Meta had placed the requirement in its new terms of service for businesses set to take effect on November 20.
Given the short timeline, Judge Guilherme Madeira Dezem issued his ruling without waiting for a response from the company.
He agreed that the damage to the media outlets would be “irreversible” once the AI were trained using their content.

“Imposing on media outlets the free and universal surrender of their copyrighted works as a toll for remaining connected to the channels through which the contemporary public consumes news constitutes a manifest abuse of rights,” he wrote in the ruling.
The judge suspended that section of the new terms of service and prohibited Meta from penalising media outlets that rejected them.
Meta will have five days after notification of the ruling to present its defence.
The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from AFP.

“The preliminary injunction is a very positive sign that there are limits to the abuse of economic power,” said Marcelo Rech, executive president of the National Association of Newspapers (ANJ), one of the plaintiffs, in a statement.
According to the associations, the ruling marks the first time in any country in favour of a coalition of media organisations opposing Meta’s new terms of service. — AFP

6306f482a642830e: AMD has predicted it will win more revenue than Intel in its next quarter, potentially marking the first time it becomes the dominant vendor whose main product is x86 processors.

The house of Zen on Tuesday announced its Q3 2026 results, which saw it grow revenue 45 percent year-over-year to $13.4 billion. The company’s Data Center segment won $8.5 billion of revenue, up 97 percent year-over-year. Sales of silicon in AMD’s client and gaming segment slid eight percent to $3.7 billion, a worse fall than the five percent fall that helped to sink Intel’s share price.
Intel, AMD’s great rival in the x86 market, offered revenue guidance of $15 billion to $16 billion for its next quarter, which would represent almost no growth.
AMD, by contrast, told investors it expects around $17 billion of revenue next quarter.
CEO Lisa Su predicted even better days are ahead.

“We think 2027 is going to be a very strong momentum year for both the CPU business as well as the data center AI business,” she said on the company’s earnings call. “We have said the overall company will grow greater than 80 percent, and for the data center CPU business, we will about double, and for the data center AI business, it will significantly more than double.”
Su said AMD is confident its supply chain can meet that demand.

“We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year,” she said. “We are also deepening our collaboration with our supply chain partners and investing alongside them to secure the long-term capacity our growth will require.”
The CEO added that AMD has “strong confidence in our ability to sustain exceptional revenue growth for years to come, with earnings growing even faster.”

If those predictions are correct, AMD will likely accelerate away from Intel to become the leading provider of x86 processors after years of challenging Chipzilla's lead. Intel would still have higher overall revenue, due to its foundry operations, but in terms of revenue earned from selling chips, AMD would become the market leader.
AMD is arguably already the server CPU technology leader, and while it is second to Nvidia in the GPU market has trounced Intel.

Even AMD's declining client and gaming revenue has an upside because it was the gaming part of the portfolio that created the problem. PC chip sales rose seven percent year-over-year to $2.9 billion. Su said strong sales of Ryzen mobile processors drove that growth.

“Commercial is becoming a larger part of our client business as large enterprises adopt Ryzen PRO PCs across their employee base,” she said, pointing to strong adoption at the world’s largest banks, automotive companies, and healthcare concerns. Big corporate buyers are often a source of bigger profits and/or steadier revenue, so AMD looks to be taking the cream off the top of the PC market rather than scrounging for SMB and retail scraps.
Investors liked what they heard, sending AMD’s share price up by around five percent in after hours trading. ®
e58ebc35f45a5c4b: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 4 — Lembaga Tabung Haji (TH) has implemented up to 76 per cent of the recommendations put forward by the Royal Commission of Inquiry (RCI) into the pilgrimage fund, the Dewan Rakyat was told today.

Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Religious Affairs) Datuk Zulkifli Hasan said TH has resolved 13 of the total recommendations under its direct responsibility, covering key operational and management areas, including overall governance improvements, financial reporting, investment and risk management, and decision-making processes.
“Among the specific actions taken based on the RCI’s findings is the full adoption of financial accounting standards in alignment with the commission’s recommendations,” he said during Question Time.
“Furthermore, since 2022, the announcement of profit distribution rates has been strictly tied to audited annual financial statements.”

Addressing issue areas surrounding excessive bonuses, forensic audits, and enforcement, the minister pointed to the RCI’s explicit recommendation to end the practice of paying overly high bonuses to staff, prompting the fund to restructure its compensation framework.

The RCI was formed by the first Pakatan Harapan administration following years of calls to investigate its finances, after allegations of mismanagement surfaced after many of the fund’s investments suffered losses.
The report was just declassified this year, with several top executives having been charged since.

Zulkifli said the amendment to the Tabung Haji Act 1995 will take into account the entire transformation based on the RCI’s recommendations, including codifying clear criteria and expertise of the board, restrictions on active politicians, and appointment processes.
The amendments would also entail the “refining” of Section 24 of the Tabung Haji Act 1995.
The minister said the proposed changes will take into account stakeholders’ input and focus on closing previously identified loopholes and weaknesses highlighted in the RCI report.

“The special committee has met three times and the technical committee five times. God willing, we will finalise it as soon as possible, and next year, we will do our best to execute the amendment to the Tabung Haji Act,” he said.
e6c055d0cc27784c: WASHINGTON, Nov 4 — Democrats won the House and were within reach of taking over the Senate in a rapidly building midterms wave yesterday projected to sweep Republicans aside and deliver a stinging repudiation of Donald Trump’s bruising presidency.

CNN and CNBC projected a Democratic House majority, giving the opposition the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration during the final two years of his presidency.

The elections were a nationwide verdict on Trump’s turbulent second term, with discontent over living costs, tariffs and the US war against Iran—which has driven fuel prices sharply higher—weighing on Republicans as his approval ratings languish near record lows.
In one of the night’s biggest shocks, Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham in South Carolina, according to media projections.

Graham was supported by Trump and had been appointed to replace her brother, longtime Republican senator Lindsey Graham, after his death in July. Democrats had not won a Senate election in the deeply conservative southern state since 1998.
The victory followed another Republican Senate loss in North Carolina, where popular former governor Roy Cooper defeated a candidate handpicked by Trump.
Democrats also held crucial Senate seats in Georgia, where rising party star Jon Ossoff won reelection, and New Hampshire, where Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the chamber.

Republicans entered election day with a 53-47 Senate majority, leaving Democrats needing four net gains to take control. With two Republican seats already flipped, the battle for the upper chamber remained unresolved.
Blue wave warning
But momentum was on the Democrats’ side.
House results offered further evidence of the scale of the Republican setback, with Democratic gains extending deep into normally conservative territory.
In a closely watched bellwether, Democrat J.D. Ford ousted Republican congresswoman Victoria Spartz in Indiana, capturing a district Trump won by 17 percentage points in 2024.
Political analysts had identified an upset in the district as an early warning that Democrats could be heading for a so-called “blue wave.”
The party also flipped a Republican-held House seat in North Carolina, while results in Florida suggested that redrawn electoral boundaries were failing to deliver the gains Republicans had expected.
In Georgia, Democratic former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in US history and ending 24 years of Republican control.

Even Republican success came after scares in unusually tight results. Trump-backed Byron Donalds won Florida’s governorship, becoming the state’s first Black governor, while Republican Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat.
Ossoff hailed the Democratic victories as a rejection of Trump’s “depravity, corruption and incompetence.”
‘Defiant’ White House
A White House official told AFP the mood around the president was “defiant,” warning that Trump would resist the “radical left” regardless of the election outcome.
“Buckle up,” the official said.

Democratic control of the House will empower congressional committees to investigate the Iran war, mass deportations and allegations of corruption, while complicating Trump’s efforts to pass new laws.

One reason is that jobs remain plentiful, with unemployment at 3.1 per cent, it said.

Stronger oil income and Petronas dividends should help Putrajaya’s finances, BMI said.
Households, however, will feel the pinch from tighter government spending policies and rising living costs.
Higher food and fuel prices are the biggest worry, as food and non-alcoholic drinks make up 25.5 per cent of household spending.
High household debt and the cost of repaying it will also hold back spending growth, BMI said.
On interest rates, BMI expects BNM to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 2.75 per cent when it announces its decision on Thursday.
It said the central bank is likely to hold off on any change to keep room to act later, given steady growth and manageable inflation.
BMI expects the rate to stay at 2.75 per cent through to 2027.

914fe66fbaac1cb7: From Moaz Nair
When political parties ride on the back of religion, it is rarely the state that suffers the most – it is the faith itself.

Globally and domestically, the dangerous fusion of the spiritual and the secular has transformed religion from an immutable moral guide into a raw tool for worldly power. When the boundary between the house of worship and the polling booth dissolves, public perception shifts. Faith becomes tethered to the behaviour of opportunistic politicians and the inevitable failures of administration. To protect the sanctity of belief, we must separate religion from partisan politics.
When politicians weaponise faith to mobilise voters, they strip it of its deeper theological and moral complexities.

Religion ceases to be a path towards spiritual growth, universal compassion or ethical governance. Instead, it is flattened into a rigid, polarising political boundary. This exploitation fosters a destructive "us versus them" mentality, making a faith that should champion justice appear intolerant, exclusionary and tribal.
A dangerous paradox

Furthermore, when political parties base their core principles on a specific doctrine, they create a dangerous paradox. If a government aligned with religion becomes corrupt, incompetent or oppressive, the public does not simply blame the politicians – they blame the religion itself. The faith is unseated from its sacred pedestal and recast as a symbol of governance failure.
To prevent this decay, several developed nations have intentionally kept political parties free of religious tags.

Turkey stands as a foundational historical blueprint. Through its secular constitutional framework, it deliberately decoupled state affairs from religious identity to protect both governance and the sanctity of personal faith.

Conversely, where religion and politics aggressively intertwine, modern history offers cautionary tales of profound public disillusionment. In some countries, decades of administrative corruption and economic mismanagement by a clerical state have severely damaged the moral authority of the faith, driving massive waves of domestic secularisation.

In the US, the tight embrace between the Christian Right and partisan factions reduced faith to a few polarising "litmus test" issues, alienating millions of moderate believers and fuelling a rapid rise in the "unchurched" population.

In India, the rise of aggressive majoritarian religious nationalism has systematically reduced vast, ancient philosophical traditions into a rigid checklist for political loyalty, fracturing communities into hostile factions.

These global shifts resonate deeply with current Malaysian political dynamics. For decades, our local landscape has seen a creeping politicisation of faith, where theological monopoly is used as a shortcut to electoral legitimacy. Political actors increasingly reduce the rich ethics of faith to divisive rhetoric and identity policing.
This local trajectory manifests in three highly destructive ways.

First, it forces a reduction of public morality. To win elections, politicians narrow expansive spiritual traditions down to a few polarising, headline-grabbing issues. This allows unqualified figures to dictate what is considered "moral" purely to suit campaign agendas.

We see this tension play out vividly in modern policy gridlocks such as the intense debates over reforming historical university admission quotas. Critical socioeconomic solutions to address specialist medical shortages were immediately hijacked and framed as a zero-sum threat to communal identity.

Second, it leads to a profound distortion of sacred texts through bureaucratic overreach. Authoritarian and populist politics frequently weaponise scriptures to justify state-sanctioned exclusion or the restriction of basic freedoms.
Instead of elevating public morality through social justice, religion is too often co-opted by state machinery as a shallow marketing proxy.

This political co-optation was starkly highlighted by the public outcry over restrictive Selangor state planning guidelines. By attempting to ban non-Muslim places of worship from commercial shop lots – a policy born out of bureaucratised hyper-regulation – the state bureaucracy treated minority faith communities not as equal partners in society, but as administrative zoning headaches.

Finally, behavioural political science confirms that intense political-religious polarisation actively drives people away from religious institutions. When observers and moderate believers see faith used as a cynical business or a hypocritical political instrument, they distance themselves from it. By transforming a universal faith into a partisan weapon, politicians end up fracturing the very communities they claim to protect.
Preserve the integrity of faith

Faith can and should be a powerful personal motivator for ethical leadership and social justice. When it truly informs politics, it elevates the state, strengthens the rule of law and fosters community under shared moral instincts. But when politics co-opts religion, faith is debased, hypocrisy breeds and polarisation thrives.

When religion is used to chase votes, it loses its soul. If we wish to preserve the integrity of faith as a universal compass for justice and peace in Malaysia, we must insulate it from the corrosive arena of partisan politics.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
